title: Research Concept
section: Supply chains are invisible — by design
text:
Supply chains are invisible — by design
Every product on the market is the end result of a chain of suppliers, sub-suppliers, raw material extractors, logistics providers, and processors — spanning dozens of countries and hundreds of companies. This chain is called a supply chain, and it is almost entirely invisible.
A typical manufacturer knows its direct suppliers — the companies it buys from directly. These are called Tier 1 suppliers. Beyond that, visibility collapses rapidly. Most companies have partial insight into their Tier 2 suppliers, and almost no knowledge of Tier 3 and beyond. The deeper you go, the darker it gets.
This is not accidental. Suppliers have strong commercial incentives to keep their own sourcing relationships confidential. Contracts, competitive pricing, and production methods are trade secrets. Even where disclosure is required by law, enforcement is weak and data is scattered across dozens of incompatible registers.
The result: a global economy built on supply chains that no one can see.

title: Research Concept
text:
The consequences are severe
This invisibility has direct, measurable consequences:
Environmental: Cobalt for electric vehicle batteries is mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo under conditions that cause severe water contamination and habitat destruction. Steel producers in Russia and Asia operate with carbon intensities multiple times higher than their European peers. Yet the companies whose products depend on these inputs often cannot name the source.
Human rights: The UK Modern Slavery Act, the German Supply Chain Act (LkSG), and the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDD) all require companies to identify and address human rights risks in their supply chains. Compliance is currently impossible beyond Tier 1 — not because companies lack the will, but because they lack the data.
Regulatory evasion: When a company knows of a cheaper, greener, or more ethical alternative to a current supplier but chooses not to act — perhaps because change is expensive, or because the current arrangement is profitable — there is presently no mechanism to detect, document, or penalise this decision. The knowledge disappears into internal memos and is never surfaced.
Innovation suppression: Researchers and policymakers cannot identify systemic inefficiencies in supply chains they cannot see. Improvement opportunities — better materials, cleaner processes, more resilient sourcing — go undiscovered.

title: Research Concept
section: This is the “holy grail” of supply chain management
text:
This is the “holy grail” of supply chain management
The term holy grail is used deliberately in supply chain literature to describe full, end-to-end supply chain visibility. It is considered holy because it has never been achieved at scale. Altana AI, a commercial platform valued at over $1 billion, has mapped approximately 50% of global trade using proprietary customs data. This represents the current state of the art — and it covers only known, disclosed transactions.
SupplyLens addresses the undisclosed portion. The nodes no one has mapped. The suppliers no one admits to. The practices no one reports.

title: Research Concept
text:
What SupplyLens does
SupplyLens is a research platform that:

Accepts a company name, product, or barcode as input
Automatically gathers open-source intelligence from trade databases, facility registries, corporate filings, news sources, and satellite data
Uses AI to infer hidden supply chain nodes — suppliers that are probable but not publicly disclosed — with an explicit, calibrated confidence score for each
Stores all findings in EDRM-compliant format — the Electronic Discovery Reference Model used in legal proceedings — with a full chain of custody for every claim
Surfaces violations, risks, and improvement opportunities detected in the graph
Generates regulatory-grade reports suitable for submission to the European Commission or national competent authorities

The platform is built entirely on existing, maintained open-source software (Neo4j, LangGraph, n8n, NeoDash, draw.io) with AI inference orchestrated through LangGraph and LiteLLM. No proprietary data sources are required.

title: Research Concept
text:
The research contribution
The core scientific contribution of SupplyLens is the multi-signal confidence fusion methodology for supply chain node inference.
When the AI infers that a particular supplier is probably part of a supply chain — even though no company has publicly disclosed this — it does not simply assert it. It combines multiple independent evidence signals, each with a calibrated weight:








Signal
Weight
Example




Trade flow data (bill of lading)
0.30
Company X shipped product Y to company Z


Facility location cross-reference
0.25
Factory within 50km of known customer


Corporate ownership structure
0.20
Subsidiary relationship via OpenCorporates


Document extraction (annual reports)
0.15
Supplier named in sustainability report


News & incident data (GDELT)
0.10
Supplier mentioned in same news context



The result is a probabilistic knowledge graph where every inferred node carries a confidence score and a full list of contributing evidence sources. This is fundamentally different from existing approaches, which rely primarily on voluntary company disclosures.

title: Research Concept
text:
Why legal admissibility matters
A supply chain map that cannot be defended in court is, for regulatory purposes, a map that does not exist. If a researcher discovers that a company knowingly suppressed a cheaper, greener alternative to a harmful material — but cannot prove it with traceable, verifiable evidence — nothing changes.
SupplyLens is designed from the ground up to produce evidence that is legally admissible. Every piece of data in the system follows the Electronic Discovery Reference Model (EDRM) — the international standard for digital evidence management used in litigation and regulatory proceedings.

title: Research Concept
text:
The chain of custody
For every claim in the SupplyLens knowledge graph, the following is recorded and immutably stored:







Stage
What is recorded




Identification
Source URL, database name, API endpoint


Preservation
SHA-256 hash of source content at time of collection


Collection
Method (scraped/API/uploaded), timestamp, software version


Processing
Extraction method, AI model version, confidence score


Review
Researcher decision (confirmed/rejected/flagged), timestamp


Analysis
Inference method, signal weights, uncertainty band


Production
Export format, recipient, case ID, export timestamp



This means: if a company challenges the findings, every claim can be traced back to a source document with a cryptographic hash proving it has not been altered.

title: Research Concept
section: How the data actually gets collected
text:
How the data actually gets collected
The EDRM pipeline runs on two tracks:
Scheduled pulls (n8n, weekly): n8n workflows automatically query ImportYeti for trade flow data, UN Comtrade for aggregate commodity flows, and OpenSupplyHub for new facility registrations. Every API response is hashed on arrival and stored in Neo4j with a full timestamp and source reference.
Triggered inference (LangGraph agent): When a researcher submits a new company or product, LangGraph orchestrates a multi-step enrichment pipeline — scraping supplier websites via Browserless, extracting text via Unstructured, querying the vector store (Qdrant) for similar known suppliers, then calling the LLM (LiteLLM/Groq) to infer probable supply chain links. Each inferred link is stored with its confidence score and the evidence that generated it.
No CrewAI or additional orchestration layer is needed — LangGraph already handles multi-step agent coordination with full state management and rollback.

title: Research Concept
text:
The enforcement loop
The practical consequence of EDRM compliance is a functioning enforcement mechanism:
Researcher discovers: Company X knew of improvement Y,
                      chose not to implement it
          ↓
Evidence: internal document (hashed), patent filing,
          sustainability report, news coverage
          ↓
EDRM report filed with European Commission
          ↓
Fine imposed, calibrated to violation severity
          ↓
Fine exceeds cost of implementing improvement
          ↓
Company implements improvement
          ↓
World is slightly better
This loop — from research finding to regulatory action to real-world change — is the ultimate purpose of SupplyLens. The tool is not an academic exercise. It is a mechanism for using evidence to make supply chains cleaner, fairer, and more transparent.

title: Research Concept
text:
Why Scania
Scania AB is a Swedish manufacturer of heavy trucks, buses, and engines with revenues exceeding €20 billion and suppliers spanning more than 50 countries. Its supply chain is deep, complex, and representative of the challenges facing the entire automotive sector.
Critically, Scania has agreed to act as a ground truth partner. This means:

Scania discloses its known Tier 1 and partial Tier 2 supplier data to the research team
SupplyLens attempts to map the same suppliers using public OSINT only
Scania validates or refutes the AI’s inferences, node by node
This validation data is used to calibrate the confidence model

This creates a rigorous, scientifically defensible validation methodology. Rather than claiming the model works in the abstract, we can demonstrate its precision and recall against a real-world ground truth.

title: Research Concept
text:
The validation phases
Phase 1 — Baseline: SupplyLens maps Scania’s Tier 1 from public sources only. Scania confirms accuracy. We establish a baseline precision/recall score.
Phase 2 — Inference: SupplyLens infers Tier 2–3 from OSINT. Scania confirms or denies each node. We calibrate the confidence weights.
Phase 3 — Unknown territory: SupplyLens maps Tier 4–5 — beyond what even Scania knows. Independent verification via trade data, investigative databases, NGO reports.
Phase 4 — Violation detection: SupplyLens flags known violations in the graph. Cross-referenced against public enforcement actions to validate detection accuracy.

title: Research Concept
text:
Geographic Map — NeoDash
The primary interface is a world map showing supply chain arcs between supplier locations. Each node represents a facility, mine, factory, or headquarters. Arcs represent material and product flows. Node colour indicates risk level; opacity indicates confidence (inferred nodes appear translucent).
Clicking a node opens an evidence panel showing everything the system knows about that supplier: confirmed facts, inferred relationships, confidence scores, source documents, and any violation flags.
Software: NeoDash (Neo4j Labs open source)

title: Research Concept
text:
Knowledge Graph — NeoDash
The second view provides an interactive network topology of the supply chain, allowing researchers to explore relationships, find shortest paths between two suppliers, identify shared dependencies across multiple products, and detect structural bottlenecks (single-source nodes).
Software: NeoDash graph view (same deployment as map, different dashboard tab)

title: Research Concept
text:
Process Flow — draw.io
The third view renders the supply chain as a BPMN-style left-to-right process diagram: raw material → processing → component → assembly → finished product. This view is used for documentation, regulatory submissions, and academic publication. Diagrams are exportable as BPMN XML, PDF, or SVG.

title: Research Concept
text:
Regulatory context
The European Union is implementing the most ambitious supply chain transparency legislation in history:

EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDD) — requires companies with 500+ employees to identify and address human rights and environmental risks throughout their supply chains
EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) — requires importers to declare the embedded carbon in imported goods
German Supply Chain Act (LkSG) — already in force, requires due diligence on environmental and human rights risks beyond Tier 1

All three regulations face the same fundamental problem: the data does not exist. Companies cannot comply with due diligence requirements for supply chain tiers they cannot see. SupplyLens directly addresses this gap.

title: Research Concept
text:
The broader vision
If SupplyLens achieves its goal — a tool that can map any supply chain from public data, infer hidden nodes with calibrated confidence, and produce legally admissible evidence of violations and suppressed improvements — the consequences extend far beyond any single case.
Researchers at any university with internet access could investigate any company’s supply chain. Journalists could verify corporate sustainability claims against independent evidence. Regulators could prioritise enforcement against the cases where evidence is strongest. Companies would know that bad practices in their supply chain are discoverable — and would act accordingly.
The information asymmetry that has protected supply chain opacity for decades would, for the first time, begin to close.

SupplyLens is developed by Research-Ready in partnership with Scania AB.

User guide: see 03-userguide.pdf

title: System Architecture
section: Signal to Action — End-to-End Data Flow
text:
Signal to Action — End-to-End Data Flow
A researcher submits a company name or product SKU. The mouth resolves the identity through GS1 and OpenCorporates, builds a list of URLs to scrape, and stores raw HTML and downloaded documents in MongoDB. That write triggers the gut: LangGraph orchestrates text extraction (Unstructured for HTML/PDF, Tika for binary formats), embedding into Qdrant, and LLM inference of probable supplier relationships. Each inferred node is scored using a weighted fusion of five OSINT signal types and written into Neo4j with a full evidence stamp — source URL, SHA-256 hash, inference method version, and confidence score. The loop repeats, following newly discovered nodes, until the depth limit is reached or no new nodes emerge.
From Neo4j, the presentation layer consumes the graph on demand. NeoDash renders supplier counts, tier breakdowns, and risk heatmaps. The evidence map plots confirmed and inferred suppliers as geographic arcs. A researcher reviewing a flagged node can pull the full EDRM package for that node — every source document, its hash, the signal weights that produced the confidence score, and any violations detected — and use it as the basis for a regulatory report submitted to a national competent authority or the European Commission.

    supplier_name  TEXT REFERENCES suppliers(neo4j_name),
    source_url     TEXT NOT NULL,
    sha256         CHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    method         TEXT,
    confidence     FLOAT,
    collected_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    reviewed_by    TEXT,
    status         TEXT DEFAULT 'unreviewed'  -- unreviewed | confirmed | rejected | flagged
);

CREATE TABLE events (
    id            SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    supplier_name TEXT,
    event_type    TEXT,
    severity      TEXT,
    event_date    DATE,
    description   TEXT,
    source_url    TEXT
);

title: Data Model
text:
Confidence Score Model
Every inferred node carries a weighted confidence score fused from five independent OSINT signals. The score is a weighted sum bounded to [0, 1]; each contributing signal is stored in the EvidenceClaim.signals[] array so the score is fully auditable.



Signal
Weight
Source




Trade flow data
0.30
UN Comtrade, ImportYeti bill-of-lading


Facility location
0.25
OpenSupplyHub, satellite imagery


Corporate structure
0.20
OpenCorporates, GLEIF LEI


Document extraction
0.15
Annual reports, sustainability filings


News & incidents
0.10
GDELT, NGO databases, ILO



A node inferred from a bill-of-lading hit (0.30) and a confirmed facility record (0.25) carries a score of 0.55 before any document or news signals are added. Scores below 0.40 are flagged as low-confidence and displayed with reduced opacity in the presentation layer. Scores above 0.80 require at least two independent signal types with no contradicting evidence.
